research_concepts: substitution rotation intervals and reconstructed lineups
methodological_questions: Does a substitution that changes the offensive five shift shot mix by more than a matched no-change placebo?
Is the shift proportional to an ex-ante, out-of-sample measure of how different the incoming and outgoing players' shot profiles are?
How can personnel effects be separated from clock, score, opponent, fatigue and coach-selected substitution timing?
Is the result informative as a positive control, or is it mechanically guaranteed?

historical_evidence.finding: Opponent lineup adaptation, with the opposing rim big off the floor. On N=1.07M possessions the shot-mix shifts were small: DRIVE +0.82pp (SE 0.25), POST_UP +0.43pp, 3PA -1.79pp (SE 0.31), rim <=4ft +0.12pp (SE 0.295, t=+0.4), PPP +0.008 (t=+1.1). The record says the verdict was WEAK/SMALL and 'will not carry a paper'. It lists LIM:small_sample and RISK:SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER.

Structural disruption vs PPP: an adequately powered null (failure mechanism B_powered_null), S3 rho=-0.040, CI [-0.212,+0.166], with MDE rho~0.23 at n=148 for S3 (n=986 overall). Validation is recorded as same_pipeline_validation only.

The Persistent Impact Score Level 1 gate failed its decay sanity check. Lifts were flat and collapsed under a within-team baseline, which the record attributes to a team-quality confound. p~0 came from n>150k with Cohen d ~0.01-0.03. It lists RISK:CONFOUNDING.

Opener recommendations were infeasible given personnel: an optimizer that ignored personnel produced targets 3-10x the stretch ceiling (C_artifact). This shows personnel constraints matter when constructing lineup-level quantities.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Detecting shot-mix shifts from a lineup condition (opposing big off floor) as a pooled possession-level comparison.
failed_approaches.why: Sub-1pp shifts, with the rim share indistinguishable from zero even on ~1.07M possessions. Recorded limitation: small sample / power.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Pooled possession-level contrasts without a within-team baseline.
failed_approaches.why: Team-quality confound produced apparent effects that vanished within team (C_artifact); large n gave p~0 for trivially small effects.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Lineup-level targets built without personnel constraints.

evidence_establishes: Under the retrieved opponent-side lineup design (FAM:SF34), shot-mix effects were small and partly indistinguishable from zero, so sub-1pp mix shifts from lineup conditions are hard to detect at the possession level.
Earlier lineup/personnel work in this project hit confounding and construction artifacts (FAM:SF-CHT-029, FAM:SF32), and p-values from very large n are not informative on their own.
A pooled, powered null on a related offense-reorganization question (FAM:SF-PAP-058) exists, with MDE rho~0.23.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether changing the team's own offensive five moves shot mix: none of the retrieved records tests that directly.
Whether a substitution-based design has the sensitivity to act as a positive control for personnel effects.
Any dose-response between player shot-profile differences and the size of the mix shift.
The size of the shift per substitution type, or its stability across seasons.
own_inferences: As worded, the claim is close to a mechanical truism: replacing a rim-running big with a wing must change who takes shots. A significant 'any change' result would show little about the design's sensitivity, and the claim could be rescued by any nonzero shift.
A meaningful positive control must pre-specify a predicted direction and magnitude from out-of-sample player shot profiles and test for dose-response, and it must beat a placebo with the same five.

FAM:SF34 suggests that when the effect operates through opponent adaptation, shifts are ~1pp. Own-five composition changes with large profile gaps (e.g., a center for a guard) should be larger, but this is untested.
Coach-selected substitution timing creates selection and context confounding (fatigue, score, foul trouble, opponent lineup), so a naive before/after comparison is biased.
The retrieved records are on possessions and reconstructed lineups, so lineup reconstruction should be validated against rotation intervals; the correspondence is not shown.
uncertainties: No retrieved record directly tests own-five shot-mix change, and I did not call follow-up tools to look for one.
Per-substitution exposure may be short: stints can be a few possessions, so shot counts per stint are small.
The share of substitutions that involve large shot-profile differences is unknown.
Rim, three-point and midrange definitions depend on shot-distance coding in the play-by-play.

historical_effect.explanation: Without history I might have approved a simple before/after test of whether shot mix changes after a lineup change. The history shifted the decision to proceed_with_changes: FAM:SF34 shows that lineup-condition mix effects can be small and underpowered, and FAM:SF-CHT-029 and FAM:SF32 show that pooled or personnel-blind contrasts produce artifacts and p~0 from huge n. The design therefore needs within-team matching, a pre-specified dose-response and a placebo, and should be judged on effect size and CI rather than p-values.

blocking_constraints.text: 'Any change in the five moves shot mix' is nearly guaranteed by construction, so as phrased it cannot fail and does not show design sensitivity. The test must be a pre-specified dose-response with placebo.

prior_work.summary: No retrieved family tests whether changing the team's own offensive five moves shot mix. The closest, FAM:SF34 (inconclusive), covers opponent-side lineup effects and found small shifts. The others contribute methodological cautions only: powered null, confounding artifacts and personnel-blind construction.

risks.text: Shot mix necessarily follows who is on the floor, so a nonzero shift is expected and uninformative. Sensitivity must be shown through predicted magnitude and dose-response.
Substitutions are coach-chosen and correlate with score, clock, fatigue, foul trouble, opponent lineup and garbage time. Team quality confounded earlier lineup work (FAM:SF-CHT-029).
Player shot profiles used to predict the shift must come from earlier data (prior season or earlier games), not from the same possessions.
Stints and per-substitution exposure are short, and sub-1pp mix effects were not detectable in FAM:SF34 even on ~1.07M possessions. Use stint windows and report an MDE.
Lineups or substitutions triggered by recent hot or cold shooting or runs can show reversion in shot mix unrelated to personnel.
Lineup reconstruction from substitutions and play-by-play can mis-assign players, especially around period starts, timeouts and simultaneous subs, and shot-zone coding may be noisy.
Conclusions rest on the placebo being valid: same-five split points and permuted substitutions must preserve context to be a fair null.
Several shot zones, substitution types and seasons invite forking paths unless the primary outcome is fixed.
Shot profiles and league shot mix shift across 2022-23 to 2024-25, so profiles and effects should be estimated with season control.

design.estimand: Within-team, within-game change in the offensive shot-mix vector (primary: share of FGA at the rim <=4ft, three-point share, and midrange share) from the 10 possessions before to the 10 after a substitution that changes the offensive five, as a function of the pre-specified predicted shift D. D is the difference between the incoming and outgoing players' shot-zone profiles, estimated only from prior-season and earlier-game data and weighted by usage. Primary parameter: slope of the realized shift on D, plus the mean shift for the top-tercile |D| substitutions. Success as a positive control requires a positive slope, with realized shifts at least a fixed fraction of predicted shifts.
design.unit: Substitution event (one team, one dead-ball stoppage, with a change to the five) nested in team-game, with possession-level shot outcomes as the underlying data. Use game-clustered or team-season-clustered SEs.
design.sample: Regular season and playoffs, 2022-23 to 2024-25. Exclude garbage time (pre-specified score margin and clock), the first and last two minutes of periods, overtime, possessions around timeouts or ejections, events with reconstruction mismatches against rotation intervals, and stints shorter than 5 possessions after the sub. Primary analysis on 2022-23 and 2023-24 for profiles and tuning, with 2024-25 as the confirmatory holdout; the profile window is fixed before outcomes are viewed.
design.power: Compute before analysis the empirical SD of the 10-possession-window rim share and the number of eligible substitution events. Report the MDE for the slope and for the top-tercile mean shift. Declare the design adequate only if the MDE is below the predicted shift for large-|D| swaps. Otherwise widen the window (15-20 possessions) or pool by substitution type. Interpret via CI and effect size, not p-values, given the large n and the FAM:SF-CHT-029 lesson.
design.controls: Team-game fixed effects, with pre-sub window shot mix, score margin, period, clock, opponent five (or opponent rim-big presence), home/away and rest as covariates. Match each large-|D| substitution to small-|D| substitutions for the same team on score and period. Estimate player profiles with shrinkage to position means. Include a season effect.
design.falsification: Placebos: (1) same-five pseudo-substitutions, splitting continuous same-five stretches at random dead-ball points and recomputing the before/after shift, which should be about 0 with slope 0 on D; (2) permuting D across substitutions within team-season, which should destroy the slope; (3) a reverse-time check that the slope on D computed from post-sub profiles does not appear in pre-sub windows. A design that finds a slope in placebos fails as a positive control. Also check that outcomes not tied to personnel (e.g., free-throw share or pace) do not scale with D.
design.multiplicity: Primary outcome: rim share, with the slope on D as the single confirmatory test. Three-point and midrange shares are secondary, with Holm correction across the three zones. Substitution-type and season subgroups are exploratory and labelled as such. No new outcomes after viewing data.
design.decision_rule: Supported (design is a valid positive control) if, on the 2024-25 holdout, the primary slope on D is positive with a 95% CI excluding 0 and at least 50% of the predicted magnitude, and the same-five placebo slope has a CI including 0 and is smaller than the real slope. Rejected if the powered CI excludes both zero and the minimum meaningful slope (design lacks sensitivity). Artifact if the placebo slope is nonzero or the effect disappears under team-game fixed effects. Uncertain if the MDE exceeds the predicted shift. A mere nonzero mean shift is not a pass.
design.data_version: NBA stats API per-game files for 2022-23, 2023-24 and 2024-25 (play-by-play, substitution rotation intervals, starters, box-score summary) as available on 2026-11-02, with possession records from the graph database built from play-by-play. Freeze the extraction date and hash, record the lineup reconstruction version, and lock the profile windows and exclusions before outcome inspection.

methodological_questions: Can a design detect personnel effects on shot mix when the offensive five changes?
How should a positive-control test be built to show a lineup-change design has power to detect effects?
How to separate personnel effects from game context, opponent, score, and clock confounding when lineups change?

system_prompt:
You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.
- explore_graph(node_id): the relationships of one graph node (a family or a question, method, dataset, measure, limitation or risk node), with neighbour labels.
- read_family(id): the complete record of one study family (for example 'FAM:SF-APPA-001').

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

Risk codes (use only these): SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, LABEL_ERROR, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY

reasoning_details.text:
I'm settling on the final answer now, since no more tools look necessary. The shot-mix-under-lineup-change idea works as a positive control, but it's close to tautological, because swapping a center for a guard mechanically changes shot mix. A control only proves the design can detect effects if it targets a known, sizable effect, and the SF34 lineup comparison came back inconclusive with an opponent-lineup effect under one point on shot mix.

I'm now weighing the evidence from past studies: an opponent-lineup effect that came in under a point, a powered null on structural disruption, and a team-quality confound that inflates significance at large n. I'm sketching a design around possession-stints that compares within-team, within-game shot-mix shifts (rim, three, midrange) against a pre-specified shot-profile distance for players entering and leaving, with placebo permutations that keep the same five on the floor.

I'm now setting the decision at proceed_with_changes with moderate-high support but low informativeness, and I'm listing the risks to guard against: confounding, a mechanical floor that makes the shift trivial, lookahead leakage from player profiles, reactive substitution, low power, drift, multiple testing, short lineup stints, and placebo dependence.

reasoning_details.text:
I'm settling on the final answer now, since no more tools look necessary. The shot-mix-under-lineup-change idea works as a positive control, but it's close to tautological, because swapping a center for a guard mechanically changes shot mix. A control only proves the design can detect effects if it targets a known, sizable effect, and the SF34 lineup comparison came back inconclusive with an opponent-lineup effect under one point on shot mix.

I'm now weighing the evidence from past studies: an opponent-lineup effect that came in under a point, a powered null on structural disruption, and a team-quality confound that inflates significance at large n. I'm sketching a design around possession-stints that compares within-team, within-game shot-mix shifts (rim, three, midrange) against a pre-specified shot-profile distance for players entering and leaving, with placebo permutations that keep the same five on the floor.

I'm now setting the decision at proceed_with_changes with moderate-high support but low informativeness, and I'm listing the risks to guard against: confounding, a mechanical floor that makes the shift trivial, lookahead leakage from player profiles, reactive substitution, low power, drift, multiple testing, short lineup stints, and placebo dependence.
